timeline.description: Moritz Fröhlich becomes a trusted mediator between porcelain and glass manufacturers and buyers for Berlin's major department stores.
timeline.longDescription: In the early 1920s, Moritz Fröhlich moved from Frankfurt on the Main to Berlin, where relatives ran a business selling knick-knacks and jewelry in Bad Strasse. He became established as a sales representative for porcelain, glass and crystal, got married and moved into a spacious apartment in Halensee. The 'Golden Twenties' saw increasing demand for inexpensive consumer goods, and Fröhlich – with his practiced eye for the market potential of simpler versions of high-quality tableware – became a trusted mediator between manufacturers and buyers for major department stores. By 1928 he employed up to three traveling sales representatives and took new premises at Ritter Strasse 59, then at number 86. The world economic crisis put the brakes on the business, and the family moved to a more modest apartment in 1930.

timeline.description: Business stays brisk with new partner Kurt Pelz – ironically taken on, perhaps, to protect the business.
timeline.longDescription: 1933 did not seem to change the business's fortunes. Fröhlich's decision to take on a non-Jewish business partner in 1934 may have been an attempt at protection – ironically, Kurt Pelz, unlike Fröhlich, resembled the stereotypical image of a Jewish businessman, and well-meaning associates promptly advised Fröhlich to get rid of 'the Jew'. Faced with increasing isolation, Jewish businesses sought out Jewish associates; Fröhlich took to leaving a Jewish newspaper protruding from his coat pocket as an inconspicuous sign of his background. Business was brisk, and in 1936 the family moved into an exclusive apartment with new furniture in Sächsische Strasse, Wilmersdorf. Just a year later they spoke openly of emigrating – but for the time being there seemed to be no rush.

timeline.description: Kurt Pelz throws Fröhlich out of his own business without compensation. After the November pogrom, the family desperately seeks a way out of Germany.
timeline.longDescription: The situation changed dramatically in 1938. 'We suddenly became Jews,' is how Moritz Fröhlich's son remembers that year. Encouraged by anti-Semitic measures and protected by anti-Semitic laws, Kurt Pelz threw Moritz Fröhlich out of his business in July without any compensation. During the pogrom in November, the relatives' stores on Bad Strasse and Olivaer Platz were demolished and Fröhlich's brother-in-law Jaschkowitz was taken to Sachsenhausen concentration camp; Fröhlich went into hiding with the help of an old colleague, Emil Busse. The family lived off its savings while he desperately looked for a place to emigrate to. When the United Kingdom turned down his immigration application, the only remaining option was the USA via Cuba. At the last moment, Fröhlich faked the date on their tickets for the St Louis so they could travel two weeks earlier on the Iberia.

timeline.description: The family reaches Havana on the Iberia – the last ship whose passengers were permitted ashore. About a quarter of the St Louis' passengers did not survive.
timeline.longDescription: On April 27, 1939, the family boarded the Iberia in Hamburg – the last ship to take passengers permitted to go ashore in Havana, while the St Louis was forced to leave Cuba after months of uncertainty with 900 despairing Jewish passengers onboard. About a quarter of the St Louis' passengers did not survive the Holocaust – including Moritz Fröhlich's sisters Esther and Recha. The Fröhlichs waited nearly two years in Cuba for permission to enter the United States, which finally came in spring 1941. In the US, Fröhlich worked briefly as a sales representative for sportswear until forced to admit his English was not proficient enough, then as an unskilled worker in a factory making army hats – fired a short time later for supporting union rights.

timeline.description: Moritz Fröhlich never re-establishes himself in business and dies in 1955. His son becomes the renowned historian Peter Gay.
timeline.longDescription:
After the war, Moritz Fröhlich tried, without much success, to set up a philatelist business with a stamp collection he had brought from Germany. He died in 1955, aged 62. 'He did his best, but in an imperceptible and insidious way, Hitler had made him a broken man.' This is how his son Peter – a renowned historian who took on the surname Gay in American exile like all his family – describes his father's fate in his autobiographical book My German Question. Growing Up in Berlin 1933–1939, published in 1998. Among the best known of his many works are two books on love and sexuality in the bourgeois age and an in-depth biography of Sigmund Freud.

The site today

The building at Konstanzer Strasse 1 in Wilmersdorf, where Moritz Fröhlich launched his business in 1924, still stands. At Ritter Strasse 86 in Kreuzberg, where Fröhlich and his partner Kurt Pelz had office premises from 1935 to 1938, the building no longer exists.
